qrdBas-c51793-d1e101.summary: Rubric introducing the single question on distinction 25 of Book 3.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether at every time it was necessary for salvation for everyone to believe explicitly and distinctly what the faithful now believe and hold.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e126.summary: First argument for the affirmative: at every time one was and is obliged to avoid error about any article of faith, which is impossible without knowing each article distinctly.
claims: Everyone is always obliged to avoid error about every article of faith.
Avoiding error about an article requires knowing it distinctly.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e137.summary: Second argument for the affirmative: infused faith has always been of the same kind (ratio) in everyone; since for some, at some time, it was necessary to believe everything distinctly according to infused faith, it was so for everyone at every time.
claims: Infused faith is always and in everyone of the same kind.
What infused faith requires of some it requires of all.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e149.summary: Third argument for the affirmative: one believer is not obliged to believe more than another, since all are equal in the faith of Christ; but pastors and doctors of the Church are obliged to believe everything distinctly and in particular, so all are. The paragraph ends with the opening words of the following contrary argument, displaced by a line break in the witness.
claims: All the faithful are equal in the faith of Christ.
Pastors and doctors are obliged to believe all articles distinctly.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e165.summary: Argument to the contrary: under the law of nature and even the written law, the mysteries of the incarnation and redemption, as they were actually accomplished, were revealed to few; so the others were not obliged to know or believe them, and even now simple believers seem not obliged to believe everything distinctly and in particular.
claims: Before Christ the mysteries of incarnation and redemption were revealed only to a few.
Those to whom something was not revealed were not obliged to believe it explicitly.
Simple believers now are not obliged to believe everything distinctly.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e183.summary: Announces that the question will be treated briefly according to the following plan.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e190.summary: First point of the plan: to show that infused faith was always necessary for salvation in anyone whatever, but that acquired faith is not.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e197.summary: Second point of the plan: whether under every state and law it was or is necessary for salvation to believe what the Church believes.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e204.summary: Third point of the plan: whether it was or is necessary that everyone believe explicitly.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e212.summary: Final point of the plan: replies to the opening arguments.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e226.summary: Determines the first article. Just as God has ordained to save no one without final grace or charity in the will, so he has ordained to save no one without infused faith; hence under every state and law, in children and adults alike, infused faith was necessary by divine ordination as an adornment, perfection, and seal of the mind, as charity is in its way. Acquired faith is different: it is not necessary for children lacking use of reason, but for adults it was necessary at least as to the act or acts through which the habit of infused faith can be generated. Every unimpeded adult saved must at some time have an act of believing in God, being bound by the affirmative precept of worshipping God to elicit acts of belief, just as they are bound to an act of loving God (as said in Book 1), each accompanied by its infused habit.
claims: By divine ordination no one is saved without infused faith, as no one is saved without charity.
Infused faith was necessary for salvation in all states and laws, for children and adults alike.
Acquired faith is not necessary for children lacking use of reason.
Every unimpeded adult must at some time elicit an act of faith in God.
The obligation to believe derives from the affirmative precept of worshipping God, parallel to the obligation to love God.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e264.summary: Determines the second article. Since infused faith has always been one and of the same kind, it was probably necessary under every state and law to believe habitually at least everything to which the Catholic, infused faith extends as its per se objects and what is per se deducible from them; this holds even of children, for whom infused faith was necessary (as Bassolis says was shown in the third article of the preceding question, though the third article of d24q1 treats the merit of belief; the point matches rather d23q1, article 1). As to the act of faith or acquired faith, children are not in question, but adults were always and are obliged to believe something, indeed briefly everything faith holds as per se objects and deducibles, though in the manner to be explained in the third article.
claims: Infused faith is numerically the same kind of faith in every state and law.
Habitually, every believer in every age believed everything to which infused faith extends.
Adults were always obliged to believe, by act, what faith holds, in a mode qualified by the third article.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e297.summary: Opens the third article with a thesis of progressive explication: faith was made explicit gradually according to the increasing perfection of the states of saved humanity, more under the written law than under the law of nature, and most perfectly in the time of the law of grace. Under the law of nature, adults were not obliged to believe explicitly everything the faith now teaches, but only what divine revelation dispensed to greater and more advanced persons, who had to believe it and publish it to lesser ones as place and time required; probably all were bound to believe explicitly that God exists and rewards the good and punishes the wicked (Hebrews), and something about a mediator who would redeem the world, though they could not identify him (Augustine, Enchiridion: no ancient could find salvation except by faith in the mediator). Under the written law, adults were bound to believe more explicitly and distinctly, as the mysteries were revealed more fully to Moses and the prophets, who had to believe and publish them, others then being bound to believe at their publication.
claims: Faith was made progressively more explicit across the law of nature, the written law, and the law of grace.
The explicitness of required faith tracks the perfection of each state.
Under the law of nature adults were bound explicitly to believe that God exists and rewards and punishes, and that a mediator would redeem the world.
Revelation was given first to more advanced persons, who were obliged to believe and to publish it.
Under the written law, what was revealed to Moses and the prophets became of obligation for others upon its publication.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e371.summary: Qualifies the account by social role. Simple and ordinary people under the written law were not bound to believe explicitly everything the pastors and doctors of the synagogue had to; it sufficed for them to believe some things explicitly and others implicitly, entrusting their faith to the synagogue and its rulers. Under the law of grace all adults must believe explicitly some articles, especially the more widely known and perceptible ones, and more than adults commonly believed under the written law (as they in turn believed more than under the law of nature); the rest they must believe at least implicitly by willing to believe what Mother Church believes in her more advanced and learned members.
claims: Simple believers under the written law could believe much only implicitly, entrusting their faith to the synagogue's leaders.
Under the law of grace all adults must believe some articles explicitly, especially the more public ones.
The required explicit content increases from the law of nature to the written law to the law of grace.
Implicit faith consists in willing to believe what the Church believes in its learned members.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e404.summary: On pastors and doctors of the Church, especially bishops and higher prelates who have the office of ruling and instructing the people: it is said that they must know explicitly everything the faith holds, at least the articles they must believe and teach, as well as the precepts of the Decalogue, mortal sins to be avoided, and similar things commonly needed for salvation or bearing on its impediment.
claims: Prelates with the office of instruction must know explicitly all articles of faith they are to teach.
They must also know the Decalogue, the mortal sins, and what commonly bears on salvation.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e426.summary: Raises whether anyone is obliged to know sacred Scripture and the controversies and errors against it, so as to avoid all errors. Bassolis answers that imposing this would be difficult and burdensome: it suffices to believe Scripture and not will to err about it, and for pastors and doctors to have some learning in it, not such that each alone knows all Scripture perfectly, but such that in the whole body of the Church, distributed across its members, there is sufficiency to exclude any error in faith and morals that arises and is brought to the Church; in this the Church has never been and, God granting, never will be found wanting. He declines to assert some of this firmly, since such matters are hard to judge and we do not know what God has determined to be necessary in particular.
claims: No individual is obliged to know all of Scripture and all controversies about it.
It suffices to believe Scripture and not will to err about it.
The sufficiency of learning to exclude error is required of the Church as a whole body, distributed across its members, not of each pastor.
The Church has never failed and will never fail in excluding error in faith and morals.
What God has determined to be necessary in particular here is uncertain.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e464.summary: Draws a parallel with mortal sin: no one is obliged to know all mortal sins, or whether every sin is mortal, since even the more advanced do not, yet everyone is obliged to avoid all mortal sins; either they know something is a mortal sin and can avoid it, or they doubt and must have recourse to the Church and conform to its judgment. Likewise, though everyone must avoid all error about the faith and Scripture, especially about the articles and what is per se deducible from them, no one must know all Scripture or every article explicitly, since one can withhold assent from what is doubtful or false until the Church's judgment has been consulted.
claims: One can be obliged to avoid all mortal sins without being obliged to know all of them.
In doubt one must defer to the Church's judgment.
Avoiding all error in faith does not require explicit knowledge of every article, because one may suspend assent pending the Church's judgment.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e505.summary: Concludes the third article: at no time was it sufficient for an adult's salvation to believe everything only implicitly and in general with nothing distinctly and explicitly; under every law an adult had to believe something explicitly, in the varying manner already described.
claims: Purely implicit faith was never sufficient for an adult's salvation.
Under every law some explicit belief was required of adults, differing in extent by state.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e518.summary: Reply to the first opening argument: what was said shows how error about every article can be avoided, even though no one is bound to believe every article in particular.
claims: Avoiding error about every article does not require believing every article in particular.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e531.summary: Reply to the second opening argument: it validly concludes that, habitually and according to infused faith, all in every state had to believe the same things in substance, since faith is of the same kind in every state; but it concludes nothing about the act of faith or about acquired faith.
claims: The sameness of infused faith establishes sameness of habitual belief across states.
It does not establish sameness of actual or acquired belief.

qrdBas-c51793-d1e544.summary: Reply to the third opening argument: one believer is not obliged to believe more than another insofar as they are a believer absolutely, but a believer who takes on the state and act of pastor or doctor is bound to believe and know more explicitly so as to exercise that office over the people. To the objection that people bound to believe their pastors would then be bound to err if misled, Bassolis replies that they are never bound to err, since they must assent to neither side of a novel proposal by a pastor or doctor until the Church has preached or taught it. To the further worry how a novice in the faith could know to withhold assent, which would seem to apply to every proposition, he leaves the reader to reflect, conceding that much in this matter is hard to resolve.
claims: Obligations to explicit faith differ by office, not by status as believer.
The faithful are never obliged to follow pastors into error.
Novel teachings of a pastor or doctor require no assent until the Church teaches them.
The problem of how a novice discerns when to withhold assent remains difficult.

qrdBas-c51793-Dd1e219.summary: Article 1 argues that, by divine ordination, infused faith is as necessary for salvation as charity, in every state and law and in children and adults alike, whereas acquired faith is not necessary for children but is for adults: every unimpeded adult saved must at some time elicit an act of believing in God, bound by the affirmative precept of worship as by the precept of love.
claims: No one is saved without infused faith, by divine ordination.
Acquired faith is required of adults but not of children.
Every unimpeded adult is obliged at some time to elicit an act of faith.

qrdBas-c51793-Dd1e279.summary: Article 2 holds that because infused faith is the same in kind across all states, everyone in every state and law habitually believed everything to which infused faith extends, including its per se objects and deducibles, even children; adults were always bound to believe by act what faith holds, in the qualified manner explained in Article 3.
claims: Habitual belief of the whole content of faith is common to every state.
Actual belief of adults is required in every state but is qualified as to explicitness.

qrdBas-c51793-Dd1e320.summary: Article 3 develops an account of the progressive explication of faith. Faith became more explicit with the perfection of each state: under the law of nature adults were bound explicitly only to God's existence and just retribution and to a coming mediator; under the written law to more, as revealed to Moses and the prophets and published by them; under the law of grace to still more. Throughout, explicit obligation was graded by role: simple believers believed much implicitly by entrusting their faith to the synagogue or to Mother Church, while pastors, especially prelates, must know explicitly the articles, the Decalogue, and the mortal sins. No individual must know all Scripture; the sufficiency to exclude error belongs to the Church as a whole body, which has never failed. As with mortal sins, one can avoid all error without knowing every article, by withholding assent and deferring to the Church in doubt. Purely implicit faith was never sufficient for an adult.
claims: Faith was made progressively more explicit across the three laws.
The extent of required explicit faith depends on both historical state and ecclesial role.
Implicit faith consists in entrusting one's faith to the Church's advanced members.
Prelates must know explicitly the articles of faith and what is commonly needed for salvation.
Sufficiency in Scriptural learning belongs to the Church corporately, not to each pastor.
Error can be avoided without explicit knowledge of all articles by suspending assent pending the Church's judgment.
Purely implicit faith never sufficed for an adult's salvation.

qrdBas-c51793-Dd1e549.summary: Replies to the three opening arguments. Avoiding error about every article does not require believing each in particular. The sameness of infused faith across states proves sameness of habitual belief but not of actual or acquired belief. Believers are equal as believers, but office imposes greater explicit obligations on pastors and doctors; the faithful are never bound to follow them into error, since they need assent to no novel teaching until the Church teaches it, though how a novice discerns this remains a hard problem.
claims: Avoiding error does not require explicit belief in every article.
Infused faith's sameness concerns habit, not act.
Greater explicit obligations follow office, not believer status.
Novel teachings of pastors require no assent until the Church teaches them.

qrdBas-c51793.summary: The single question on Book 3, distinction 25 asks whether at every time it was necessary for salvation for everyone to believe explicitly and distinctly what the faithful now believe. Against arguments from the duty to avoid all error, the sameness of infused faith, and the equality of believers, and with a contrary argument that the mysteries were revealed only to a few before Christ, Bassolis answers in three articles. Infused faith, like charity, was always necessary by divine ordination for everyone, while acquired faith and the act of believing are necessary only for adults, who are bound to elicit acts of faith by the precept of worship. Habitually, all in every state believed the whole content of infused faith. Actually and explicitly, however, faith was unfolded progressively across the law of nature (God, retribution, a coming mediator), the written law, and the law of grace, and the required explicitness is graded by role: simple believers may believe much implicitly by entrusting their faith to the Church, while prelates must know the articles, the Decalogue, and mortal sins explicitly. Scriptural sufficiency belongs to the Church corporately; individuals avoid error by suspending assent and deferring to the Church in doubt. Purely implicit faith never sufficed for an adult. The replies distinguish habit from act and believer from office, and hold that the faithful are never bound to follow pastors into novel error.
claims: Infused faith was necessary for salvation in every state and for everyone.
Acquired, actual faith is necessary for adults, who must at some time elicit an act of faith.
Habitually all believers of every age believed the same content; explicitly, faith was unfolded progressively across the three laws.
Required explicit faith varies by historical state and by ecclesial office.
Simple believers may believe much implicitly by entrusting their faith to the Church.
Purely implicit faith was never sufficient for an adult's salvation.
The faithful are never bound to follow pastors into error and should withhold assent from novelties pending the Church's teaching.
